title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome, or Lowe syndrome, is a rare X-linked recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the OCRL gene, leading to disruption of phosphoinositide metabolism and widespread cellular dysfunction. This course reviews this condition, which affects multiple organ systems, producing a characteristic triad of congenital cataracts, intellectual disability, and proximal renal tubular dysfunction, as well as the neurological manifestations of oculocerebrorenal syndrome, including hypotonia, seizures, and behavioral disturbances. Additionally, renal involvement progresses to chronic kidney disease. Ocular findings such as bilateral cataracts and infantile-onset glaucoma that frequently cause severe visual impairment and the need for supportive, interprofessional management for optimizing function and quality of life are also discussed.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course explores the molecular pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnostic strategies, and management principles of oculocerebrorenal syndrome. Participants also gain an in-depth understanding of the roles of the OCRL gene and its enzyme product, OCRL-1, in regulating intracellular trafficking and cytoskeletal organization. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in early recognition of systemic involvement, evidence-based approaches for managing ocular and renal complications, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to optimize long-term outcomes for patients affected by this complex multisystem disorder.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate Oculocerebrorenal syndrome from other causes of failure to thrive and congenital cataracts based on clinical, ocular, and systemic features. Identify key genetic and phenotypic markers that aid in timely diagnosis and individualized management planning. Assess the role of early interprofessional intervention in improving long-term visual, renal, and neurodevelopmental outcomes in affected children. Enhance the interprofessional approach in the diagnosis, management, and long-term care of patients with oculocerebrorenal syndrome by fostering collaboration among pediatricians, ophthalmologists, nephrologists, geneticists, and allied health professionals. title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome, more commonly referred to as Lowe syndrome, was first described in the early 1950s by Lowe and colleagues, who identified a constellation of findings in affected children, including intellectual disability, organic aciduria, reduced renal ammonia production, bilateral cataracts, and glaucoma. [1] Subsequent studies have further delineated the disorder, noting the presence of Fanconi-type proximal renal tubulopathy, generalized areflexia, and characteristic arthropathy. [2] [3] The condition is now established as an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the OCRL gene, leading to disturbances in phosphoinositide metabolism and widespread impairment of intracellular trafficking and cytoskeletal organization. These molecular derangements explain the syndrome’s broad involvement of ocular, neurological, and renal systems. [4]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Introduction
content: The syndrome primarily affects the lens and trabecular meshwork in the eye, resulting in congenital cataracts and infantile-onset glaucoma. [5] In the central nervous system, abnormalities in synaptic signaling and white matter integrity underlie the intellectual disability, hypotonia, and seizures observed in many patients. Renal manifestations arise from dysfunction of the proximal tubules, producing a partial Fanconi syndrome characterized by bicarbonaturia, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, and progressive chronic kidney disease. [6]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Introduction
content: The natural history of oculocerebrorenal syndrome typically begins in the neonatal period, characterized by severe muscular hypotonia and ocular abnormalities, which serve as the earliest diagnostic indicators. [4] Renal manifestations generally evolve more gradually, with incomplete Fanconi syndrome becoming evident in infancy or early childhood. Over time, the progression of renal disease culminates in chronic kidney failure, which remains the leading cause of mortality. Life expectancy is limited, with most patients surviving into the third or fourth decade of life. [3] Early diagnosis and supportive care are crucial for preventing life-threatening complications and maximizing the quality of life. [3]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Etiology
content: The oculocerebrorenal syndrome is caused by mutations in the OCRL gene, which is mapped to chromosome Xq25–26. [7] [8] The OCRL gene encodes the enzyme OCRL-1, an inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase, that primarily converts phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate. [4] OCRL-1 is localized to clathrin-coated pits on the plasma membrane, as well as to multiple intracellular organelles, including endosomes and the trans-Golgi network. [9] [10] Through these localizations, OCRL-1 regulates endocytic trafficking, Golgi-to-endosome transport, actin cytoskeleton remodeling, and polarized cell maturation, processes that are essential for cellular protein sorting, signaling, and structural integrity. [11] [10]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Etiology
content: The mutation spectrum of OCRL is broad, with more than 200 pathogenic variants reported. [12] The majority are frameshift, nonsense, or splice-site mutations that lead to mRNA instability or premature protein truncation. [13] Missense mutations and larger genomic deletions account for a smaller proportion of cases. [14] [15] The OCRL mutation exhibits considerable phenotypic heterogeneity. [16]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Etiology
content: The inheritance pattern of oculocerebrorenal syndrome is X-linked recessive. [17] Affected males typically inherit the pathogenic variant from carrier mothers, although de novo mutations account for up to one-third of cases. [18] Female carriers are usually asymptomatic, but approximately 95% of those older than 15 years exhibit subtle but characteristic radial lenticular opacities on slit-lamp examination. [8] [6] In rare instances, female carriers may manifest systemic features of oculocerebrorenal syndrome, particularly in the presence of cytogenetic or epigenetic alterations. Such scenarios include a 45, X karyotype, skewed X-inactivation favoring the mutant allele, compound heterozygosity for 2 pathogenic variants, or X-autosome translocations disrupting OCRL . [19] [6] [8]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Recent evidence suggests that INPP5B, a closely related inositol 5-phosphatase paralog of OCRL-1, may act as a functional modifier in oculocerebrorenal syndrome and Dent disease type 2. [20] In addition to oculocerebrorenal syndrome, mutations in OCRL can result in a rare X-linked recessive condition known as Dent disease type 2. This allelic disorder has a milder phenotype and is caused by missense variants distributed across exons 9 to 21, while truncating mutations tend to cluster in exons 1 to 7. [19] Patients with Dent disease type 2 typically present with isolated renal Fanconi syndrome, low molecular weight proteinuria, and hypercalciuria without the classic extrarenal features, including ocular or neurological manifestations of oculocerebrorenal syndrome. [4] Ocular features are uncommon in Dent disease type 2 and include mild nuclear cataracts, which are usually not visually significant. Typically, proximal renal tubular acidosis is not seen in Dent disease type 2. [21]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome is a rare disorder, with an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 500,000 in the general population. [3] This condition occurs almost exclusively in males and, within the United States, has been reported to affect between 1 and 10 males per million. [3]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome results from mutations in the OCRL gene, which encodes the inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase OCRL-1. A deficiency of this enzyme disrupts phosphoinositide metabolism, leading to the abnormal accumulation of PIP2 and impairing key cellular processes, including endocytosis, vesicular trafficking, actin cytoskeleton remodeling, cell polarity, and ciliogenesis. [11] [10] These defects are particularly detrimental in highly polarized cells, eg, renal proximal tubular epithelium, neurons, and lens epithelial cells, which explains the characteristic multisystem involvement. [22] The most common clinical manifestations include congenital cataracts, infantile glaucoma, hypotonia with delayed motor development, intellectual disability, and a progressive Fanconi-type proximal renal tubulopathy leading to chronic kidney disease. [3]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Patients with oculocerebrorenal syndrome exhibit defects across several organ systems. The triad of congenital cataracts, cognitive impairment, and proximal renal tubular dysfunction classically defines it. [23] The syndrome's varying clinical manifestations are associated with the following organ systems.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Nervous System
content: Neurological involvement is a leading cause of morbidity in oculocerebrorenal syndrome, with both the central and peripheral nervous systems affected. Early features commonly include profound hypotonia and reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes. [3] Feeding difficulties are common in infancy, often due to weak or ineffective sucking. Hypotonia contributes to the delayed attainment of motor milestones, eg, independent ambulation. Seizures may develop and can vary widely in type and severity, while intellectual disability is present in most patients, ranging from mild to severe. [24] Additionally, behavioral disturbances are also common, with many patients exhibiting aggression, obsessive-compulsive traits, temper outbursts, and other conduct disorders that impair social and daily functioning and may result in self-injury (including head banging). [25] [26]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Ocular System
content: The visual prognosis in patients with oculocerebrorenal syndrome is generally poor, largely due to the coexistence of multiple ocular abnormalities. The hallmark finding is bilateral congenital cataracts, which develop in utero and are typically addressed with cataract surgery during infancy. [27] [28] Cataract formation is believed to result from a genetic defect interfering with the migration of crystalline lens epithelial cells. [29] Although not specific to oculocerebrorenal syndrome, these children may have associated posterior lenticonus. [29]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Ocular System
content: In addition, some patients develop X-linked infantile glaucoma, with or without buphthalmos, usually within the first few decades of life. This glaucoma is challenging to manage and has been identified as one of the major causes of blindness in oculocerebrorenal syndrome. [30] [5] Infantile glaucoma affects around 50% of patients and can be challenging to treat. [6] Patients are often on multiple topical medications.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Ocular System
content: Surgical intervention may be necessary for more effective control of intraocular pressure. In a case series, Shah and colleagues reported distinct anatomic differences in glaucomatous patients with oculocerebrorenal syndrome. These differences include a deeper and wider anterior chamber, a thinner and steeper cornea, a wider angle, a more reflective and tapered iris, and a thinner, narrower, and flatter lens compared to those without glaucoma. [31]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Ocular System
content: Other notable complications of oculocerebrorenal syndrome include the development of conjunctival or corneal keloids, which may lead to visually significant corneal scarring. [32] Because of this risk, contact lenses are generally avoided in these patients. Additional ophthalmic features that have been described include microphthalmos, enophthalmos, band-shaped keratopathy, retinal dystrophy, nystagmus, strabismus, and amblyopia. [6] Radial lenticular opacities involving all cortical layers are characteristic of female OCRL gene carriers and serve as an important ophthalmologic marker for carrier detection. [33] [8]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Ocular System
content: Recent insights from a cohort of southern Chinese patients broaden the known phenotypic and genetic spectrum of oculocerebrorenal syndrome. In a study of 8 affected children, 5 novel variants of OCRL were identified. [14] Of these, 3 nonsense mutations were confirmed as pathogenic, and 2 missense variants of uncertain significance were associated with classic severe phenotypes. Notably, a patient did not present with congenital cataracts, challenging the assumption that ocular features are always present at birth and illustrating an atypical presentation in oculocerebrorenal syndrome. [14]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Renal System
content: In oculocerebrorenal syndrome, the renal involvement is defined by Fanconi syndrome with proximal tubular dysfunction and progression to renal failure. Although renal disease is not always evident at birth, it typically becomes apparent in early infancy. Impaired endocytosis within the proximal tubules leads to low-molecular-weight proteinuria, including beta-2-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein, and the lysosomal enzyme N-acetyl glucosaminidase, often reaching the nephrotic range. [4] Low-molecular-weight proteinuria serves as an early indicator of renal involvement and has been detected as soon as the neonatal period. [34]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Renal System
content: Patients are also predisposed to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Increased urinary excretion of amino acids and calcium is commonly observed, with hypercalciuria leading to nephrolithiasis in approximately half of affected individuals. Renal calculi usually consist of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate. [35] Ongoing phosphate wasting contributes to the development of rickets and osteomalacia. [36]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Renal System
content: Chronic, progressive renal failure remains a central feature of oculocerebrorenal syndrome and necessitates regular monitoring of renal function. By the fourth decade of life, the majority of patients reach stage 4 to 5 chronic kidney disease. [35] [37]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- The Musculoskeletal System
content: Musculoskeletal manifestations of oculocerebrorenal syndrome include osteopenia, tenosynovitis, and debilitating arthropathy. [38] Osteopenia can be exacerbated by hypophosphatemia and metabolic acidosis, further resulting in pathologic fractures. [4] These patients are also prone to stunted growth and short stature, which has been postulated to be the result of growth hormone deficiency. [39] Scoliosis has also been reported in these patients and may worsen with age. [40]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Other Clinical Features
content: Dermatologic findings reported in patients with oculocerebrorenal syndrome include benign cystic lesions, thought to originate from hair follicles. [41] The etiology of these skin lesions is poorly understood but has been attributed to elevated levels of lysosomal enzymes in extracellular tissue. [42] Dental anomalies, including delayed tooth eruption, enamel hypoplasia, and tooth impaction, have also been reported in oculocerebrorenal syndrome. [43] Multiple odontogenic keratocysts have also been reported in a patient with oculocerebrorenal syndrome. [44]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Other Clinical Features
content: About one-third of males have cryptorchidism. [45] However, puberty and testosterone levels are reportedly normal in most patients. Delayed platelet activation can also lead to dysfunction of primary hemostasis. [46] Infrequently, patients may have facial dysmorphism. Facial features include frontal bossing, deep-set eyes, and chubby cheeks. Individuals may also have a fair complexion and a long face. [3]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: Infants with clinical features suggestive of oculocerebrorenal syndrome (particularly male infants presenting with congenital cataracts, hypotonia, or failure to thrive) must undergo a thorough laboratory evaluation. Serum and urine studies may demonstrate metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, elevated creatinine, proteinuria, hypercalciuria, and aminoaciduria, all of which are consistent with proximal tubular dysfunction. [4] Additional diagnostics may be indicated if other systemic symptoms or findings are present.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: In cases where neurological involvement is suspected, neuroimaging may be helpful. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) often reveals periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted sequences, and mild ventriculomegaly may also be observed. [47]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Molecular Studies
content: The definitive diagnosis is established through molecular genetic testing, which involves identifying a pathogenic variant in the OCRL gene. Reduced inositol polyphosphate-5-phosphatase activity can also be demonstrated in cultured skin fibroblasts. Antenatal diagnosis is possible when oculocerebrorenal syndrome is suspected: ultrasound may detect fetal cataracts, and elevated maternal serum or amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein levels can provide additional supportive evidence. [27] [48]

The definitive diagnosis is established through molecular genetic testing, which involves identifying a pathogenic variant in the OCRL gene. Reduced inositol polyphosphate-5-phosphatase activity can also be demonstrated in cultured skin fibroblasts. Antenatal diagnosis is possible when oculocerebrorenal syndrome is suspected: ultrasound may detect fetal cataracts, and elevated maternal serum or amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein levels can provide additional supportive evidence. [27] [48]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: The oculocerebrorenal syndrome has systemic manifestations that can impact patient morbidity and mortality. Treatment focuses on optimizing system functions and preventing acute illness.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- The Nervous and Musculoskeletal System Management
content: Management of hypotonia in oculocerebrorenal syndrome relies on early initiation of physical therapy and structured rehabilitation programs, which are essential to improve motor function and prevent long-term disability. [3] Maintaining joint mobility through regular physiotherapy may help reduce the risk of developing contractures and lead to better musculoskeletal outcomes. [6] Prevention and treatment of osteomalacia are achieved with oral supplementation of vitamin D (calcitriol) and phosphate, addressing the underlying metabolic disturbances. In cases where hypotonia leads to significant dysphagia and impaired oral intake, enteral feeding via nasogastric or gastrostomy tube may be required to ensure adequate nutrition.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- The Nervous and Musculoskeletal System Management
content: Seizure management is tailored to the individual, with anticonvulsant therapy initiated as clinically indicated. Behavioral and psychiatric manifestations are frequent and best addressed through an interprofessional approach, incorporating medical, psychological, and educational interventions. Comprehensive care may involve special education programs, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy to optimize developmental progress and daily functioning. Pharmacologic agents, eg, antipsychotics and antidepressants, should be individualized alongside supportive care. [3]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- The Ocular System Management
content: Congenital cataracts require early surgical intervention, ideally in infancy, to prevent amblyopia and optimize visual outcomes. [50] Due to the small size of their globes, these infants are left aphakic and prescribed relevant aphakic refractive correction. [51] Intraocular lens implantation, especially in these small, vulnerable eyes, can increase the risk of developing glaucoma. Moreover, glaucoma in oculocerebrorenal syndrome is often recalcitrant to treatment and requires further surgical intervention. Contact lenses are not the preferred method of aphakia correction in these patients, as they may increase the risk of corneal keloid formation. [6]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- The Ocular System Management
content: These children are to be serially followed up to monitor for changes in refractive error and growth of axial length as the child grows, in addition to checking for postoperative complications, eg, visual axis opacification and aphakic glaucoma. In patients with oculocerebrorenal syndrome who develop infantile or aphakic glaucoma, intraocular pressures are often challenging to control with medical therapy alone. In many cases, surgical management is necessary.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- The Ocular System Management
content: The most commonly reported glaucoma surgeries performed in this patient population are trabeculectomy and goniotomy. The other common glaucoma surgery in these patients is aqueous tube shunt implantation. Patching or extraocular muscle surgery is used to treat patients with strabismus. Corneal keloids can be surgically removed, particularly if they compromise visual acuity. However, some patients suffer from corneal scarring or require corneal transplantation. [5] Decreased vision secondary to corneal scarring also increases the risk of amblyopia.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- The Renal System
content: Alkali therapy, most commonly with sodium bicarbonate, is essential in the management of acidemia. Regular monitoring of serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels is necessary to prevent excessive vitamin D supplementation, which can exacerbate hypercalciuria and increase the risk of nephrolithiasis. [3] For patients who progress to end-stage renal disease, dialysis becomes necessary, although reports of kidney transplantation in oculocerebrorenal syndrome remain limited. [52]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: The severity of ocular, renal, and systemic complications largely determines the prognosis of oculocerebrorenal syndrome. [6] Visual outcomes are generally poor due to the high risk of amblyopia and the frequent development of severe, difficult-to-control glaucoma, even after cataract surgery. In oculocerebrorenal syndrome, about 50% of males develop infantile glaucoma, often refractory to medical therapy, and corrected visual acuity is rarely better than 20/100. [6]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: Neuromuscular complications, particularly hypotonia, can cause significant dysphagia, sometimes necessitating tube feeding, and increase vulnerability to respiratory infections. Renal disease is a progressive condition that varies in severity, typically worsening with age. Chronic renal failure remains the leading cause of mortality, while other common contributors to reduced life expectancy include seizures, respiratory illness, and recurrent infections. Most patients survive into the second to fourth decade of life, although outcomes are highly variable and depend on early recognition, interprofessional management, and vigilant monitoring of systemic complications. [4]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Complications
content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome involves multiple organ systems, and its complications substantially affect the overall quality of life. Ocular complications include congenital cataracts, which can cause amblyopia if untreated. Cataract surgery itself carries a risk of secondary aphakic glaucoma, which is often severe and challenging to manage. [53] Neuromuscular complications, eg, hypotonia, contribute to delayed motor development, feeding difficulties, and dysphagia, increasing the risk of respiratory infections and aspiration. Neurological complications may include seizures and febrile convulsions, which can vary in severity.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Complications
content: Renal complications arise from proximal tubular dysfunction, leading to excessive loss of minerals and electrolytes, which can cause failure to thrive, growth retardation, and hypophosphatemic rickets. Hypercalciuria increases the chances of kidney stones. Hematologic and surgical risks include impaired hemostasis and mild thrombocytopenia, which may increase the likelihood of intraoperative bleeding during procedures. [46] [54] Collectively, these complications underscore the importance of vigilant, interprofessional monitoring, early intervention, and individualized management to optimize outcomes and minimize morbidity in affected patients. [46]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Due to the multisystem involvement of oculocerebrorenal syndrome, structured and lifelong surveillance is critical to detect complications early and optimize outcomes. To ensure good visual acuity, intraocular pressure should be monitored at least every 6 months throughout life to detect and manage glaucoma, which may be severe and resistant to treatment. [6] Additional eye evaluations, including visual acuity testing, corneal health assessment, and fundus examination, should be performed at intervals determined by the treating ophthalmologist, based on disease severity and surgical history.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: In patients undergoing cataract surgery, postoperative care and rehabilitation are essential to optimize outcomes. Close and structured follow-up is necessary, primarily through serial examinations under anesthesia. These examinations under anesthesia are crucial for accurate refraction and prescription of corrective lenses, monitoring axial length growth and stabilization, and determining the optimal timing for secondary intraocular lens implantation. Since examining young or developmentally delayed children in clinic settings is often challenging, examinations under anesthesia also play a critical role in the early detection of postsurgical complications, eg, glaucoma, posterior capsular opacification, or inflammation. This tailored approach helps optimize visual outcomes and supports overall neurodevelopment in this vulnerable population.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Renal monitoring is equally important, as tubular dysfunction and progression to chronic kidney disease are leading contributors to morbidity and mortality. Patients should undergo annual assessments (at least) of kidney function, including serum electrolyte levels, renal imaging, and urine studies. [6] Growth and developmental progress should also be tracked annually to guide interventions such as nutritional support, physiotherapy, and special education services.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: The increased risk of musculoskeletal complications, including scoliosis and joint laxity, warrants an annual evaluation by an orthopedic specialist. [6] This enables the timely identification of spinal deformities or joint contractures that may interfere with mobility and quality of life. Lastly, dental care is also a key component of surveillance. Semiannual dental examinations are recommended to prevent caries, manage dental structural anomalies, and promote oral health. This coordinated surveillance framework ensures early recognition of complications across multiple systems, facilitates timely interventions, and supports a proactive, interprofessional approach to patient care.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Consultations
content: Patients with oculocerebrorenal syndrome require interprofessional care due to the involvement of multiple organ systems. Key consultations typically include pediatric nephrology for managing proximal renal tubular dysfunction and monitoring electrolyte imbalances, pediatric neurology for hypotonia, seizures, and developmental support, and ophthalmology for congenital cataracts, glaucoma, and other visual issues. Additional input from clinical genetics is crucial for accurate diagnosis, effective counseling, and informed family planning. Meanwhile, physical, occupational, and speech therapy support motor development and address feeding difficulties. Behavioral and psychiatric evaluation may also be necessary to address conduct disorders and adaptive functioning challenges. [55]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome is a rare X-linked recessive disorder, most commonly affecting males, with about one-third of cases resulting from de novo mutations. [56] Affected males have not been reported to reproduce, but family members should be offered genetic counseling to understand inheritance patterns, recurrence risks, and implications for future pregnancies. [6] Prenatal genetic testing can assist in identifying at-risk fetuses, particularly for women with previously affected children, as germline mosaicism may occur.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Given the multisystemic nature of oculocerebrorenal syndrome, ongoing education for patients and caregivers is critical. Families should be informed about early complications (eg, hypotonia), which can cause feeding difficulties and delayed motor development. Awareness of potential behavioral and conduct disorders, including aggression, obsessive-compulsive tendencies, and self-injurious behaviors, is essential, particularly in children with low vision and cognitive impairment. [55] Parents and caregivers should receive guidance on early intervention strategies, including individualized behavior modification programs, physical and occupational therapy, and appropriate pharmacologic management when indicated. Educating families on these aspects empowers them to recognize early warning signs, adhere to monitoring schedules, and actively participate in the child’s interprofessional care, thereby helping to mitigate complications and improve long-term outcomes. [55]

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome should be suspected in any male infant presenting with the triad of congenital cataracts, severe hypotonia, and evidence of proximal renal tubular dysfunction. Early ophthalmologic evaluation is crucial, as cataract extraction in infancy can significantly improve visual development and reduce the risk of amblyopia. Timely detection and management of glaucoma are also essential to preserve residual vision. Hypotonia may improve gradually with age but often results in delayed motor milestones, requiring long-term physiotherapy and supportive care.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: A common pitfall is misdiagnosis as isolated congenital cataracts or nonspecific developmental delay before renal features become apparent. [3] Careful slit-lamp examination of carrier females can help identify at-risk families through the presence of characteristic radial lenticular opacities. Recognition of Dent disease type 2 as an allelic disorder is also essential, as it may be confused with the renal presentation of oculocerebrorenal syndrome, but lacks the extrarenal manifestations characteristic of oculocerebrorenal syndrome. [57]

content: From a preventive standpoint, genetic counseling plays a critical role. Carrier detection and prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing can inform family planning and help reduce the risk of recurrence. Interprofessional management, encompassing nephrology, ophthalmology, neurology, physiotherapy, and pediatrics, is crucial for enhancing quality of life and preventing complications, eg, end-stage renal disease.

content: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome is a rare X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the OCRL gene, leading to disruptions in phosphoinositide metabolism that affect ocular, neurological, and renal systems. The disease typically presents in infancy with congenital cataracts, hypotonia, and evolving renal dysfunction, progressing to chronic kidney disease. Because of its complex, multisystem nature, patients require lifelong, interprofessional management focused on early diagnosis, prevention of complications, and optimization of function and quality of life.

title: Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Management of oculocerebrorenal syndrome relies on coordinated collaboration among an interprofessional healthcare team. Physicians from ophthalmology, nephrology, neurology, and endocrinology monitor disease progression and guide evidence-based interventions. Advanced practitioners, nurses, and pharmacists support treatment adherence, manage comorbidities, and educate families. Geneticists and counselors provide essential guidance on inheritance and testing, while therapists address developmental, motor, and behavioral challenges. Effective communication, shared documentation, and ethical decision-making ensure continuity, enhance patient safety, and strengthen outcomes through cohesive, patient-centered, team-based care. [4]
